meta_story.title: The Making of Computing
meta_story.description:
Computing pioneers transformed calculation from a laborious human task into a general-purpose medium for science, government, business, communication, and creativity. In the nineteenth century, Charles Babbage and Ada Lovelace imagined machines that could follow symbolic instructions; Herman Hollerith demonstrated that information itself could be sorted and counted at industrial scale. Their ideas supplied a vocabulary of programs, data, memory, and automation before electronic computers existed.

The twentieth century turned those concepts into working machines and then placed them in front of millions of people. Wartime codebreaking and electronic design accelerated the stored-program computer, while compiler research made programming more reliable and accessible. Interactive systems, conversational software, compact business computers, and elegantly designed personal devices redirected computing toward human needs, while critics such as Joseph Weizenbaum pressed the public to ask what decisions machines should and should not make.

chapters.title: Engines for Information (1822-1890)

person_events.theme_connection: Errors in mathematical and astronomical tables led Charles Babbage to propose the Difference Engine. It would calculate tables through a repeatable sequence of mechanical operations.
Babbage began plans for the Analytical Engine after work on the Difference Engine stalled. The new design combined operations, memory, and controlled instructions in a general calculating machine.

person_events.event_title: Lovelace Publishes Her Analytical Engine Notes
person_events.theme_connection: Ada Lovelace translated Luigi Menabrea’s account of the Analytical Engine and added seven extensive notes. They included a method for calculating Bernoulli numbers and described how the machine could manipulate symbols representing information beyond numbers.
Herman Hollerith received U.S. Patent 395,782 for recording separate statistical facts as holes in cards. Electrically operated mechanical counters read and counted the encoded data.
The United States Census Office used Hollerith’s machines to process records for 62,979,766 residents. Automated sorting and counting brought machine data processing to a national scale.

chapters.lead_in: The earliest designs treated calculation as a sequence that machinery could perform. Punched cards then carried encoded records into large government operations.

chapters.title: Programs Under Pressure (1900-1945)

person_events.theme_connection: The Census Office again used Hollerith tabulators for the national census. His Tabulating Machine Company also leased punched-card equipment to census bureaus and commercial customers in several countries.
Hollerith introduced the Type I Tabulator with a rewiring control panel. Operators could configure the same machine for different punched-card jobs.
Vannevar Bush began building a mechanical differential analyzer at MIT. The machine automated the solution of differential equations and built on Herbert R. Stewart’s earlier integraph.

Alan Turing published On Computable Numbers, with an Application to the Entscheidungsproblem. Its universal machine supplied a mathematical model for any symbolic procedure that could be expressed as defined steps.

Konrad Zuse completed the mechanical Z1 in his parents’ Berlin apartment with help from Helmut Schreyer. The programmable machine did not operate reliably, but it put automatic general calculation into physical form.
At Bletchley Park, Turing specified the British bombe for searching possible Enigma settings. Gordon Welchman’s diagonal board improved the search, which built on earlier Polish cryptanalytic work.

Turing took charge of Hut 8, the section responsible for German naval Enigma traffic. He worked with Joan Clarke and other cryptanalysts and developed Banburismus to reduce the bombe’s search workload.
Zuse presented the relay-based Z3 in Berlin with Helmut Schreyer. The programmable computer performed automatic calculations for work supported by a German aviation research organization.
While working on the Z4, Zuse designed Plankalkül as a formal language for expressing algorithms independently of one machine. Wartime conditions kept the design unpublished.

After his wartime work, Turing joined the National Physical Laboratory and drafted the Automatic Computing Engine. The design specified a high-speed electronic computer with instructions stored in memory.

John von Neumann circulated First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC after discussions with Herman Goldstine, John Mauchly, and J. Presper Eckert. The report described an electronic computer that kept data and instructions in shared memory.

Vannevar Bush published As We May Think and described the memex, a proposed microfilm system for storing documents and notes. Its associative links offered a model for navigating connected information.

historical_context.title: World War II
historical_context.description: World War II was the global war fought by the Allied and Axis powers from 1939 to 1945. It sent Alan Turing to Bletchley Park for cryptanalysis, placed Vannevar Bush in charge of coordinating U.S. military research, and disrupted Konrad Zuse's computer work in wartime Germany.

chapters.lead_in: Flexible tabulators, analog calculators, and programmable machines emerged from government, academic, and industrial work. War gave automated searches and electronic designs immediate purposes.

chapters.title: Computers Learn New Work (1946-1968)

person_events.theme_connection: Von Neumann directed the Institute for Advanced Study computer project with Julian Bigelow and Herman Goldstine. Their stored-program machine began operating in 1952 and became a model for later scientific computers.
Turing and David Champernowne devised Turochamp, a program for playing chess. No available computer could run it at a useful speed, so they worked through its moves by hand.
In Computing Machinery and Intelligence, Turing proposed the Imitation Game. A human judge would exchange text with a person and a computer and try to identify which was the machine.

person_events.event_title: Installs the Z4 at ETH Zurich
person_events.theme_connection: Zuse installed the programmable Z4 at ETH Zurich under a rental agreement arranged with Eduard Stiefel. Researchers used it for numerical work that included calculations for a dam project.
Grace Hopper completed a program linker for the A-0 System and called it a compiler. It assembled reusable symbolic instructions into operations a computer could execute.
Eckert–Mauchly chose Hopper to lead its automatic-programming department. Her group released compiled languages including FLOW-MATIC, which used readable statements for business data processing.

Heinz Nixdorf directed development of the ES with Alfred Wierzoich and technical assistance from Walter Sprick. His laboratory delivered the electronic calculating computer to RWE’s accounting department in Essen.

While preparing a demonstration for the ARMAC computer, Edsger W. Dijkstra formulated a method for finding the shortest path through a network. The resulting algorithm became a basic tool for routing and graph analysis.
Hopper served as a technical consultant to the CODASYL committee as it developed COBOL. The language let business programs run on machines from different manufacturers.

Dijkstra and Jaap A. Zonneveld completed an ALGOL 60 compiler at Amsterdam’s Mathematical Centre. They kept duplicate notes in separate places while working day and night to preserve the design if one record was lost.
Douglas Engelbart published Augmenting Human Intellect at Stanford Research Institute. The report proposed interactive workstations for organizing and sharing information.
Engelbart developed the computer mouse at his Augmentation Research Center. Lead engineer Bill English built the first prototype from Engelbart’s notes and became its first user.
Joseph Weizenbaum began developing ELIZA at MIT in the SLIP list-processing language. Its DOCTOR script generated replies modeled on a Rogerian psychotherapist.

Dijkstra introduced semaphores while studying how several computer processes could share resources safely. The programming construct coordinates access so concurrent processes do not interfere with one another.

person_events.event_title: Unveils Wanderer Logatronic at Hanover Fair
person_events.theme_connection: Nixdorf presented the Wanderer Logatronic at the Hanover Fair. Otto Müller designed the modular desk computer with solid-state electronic components.

Frances Allen published Program Optimization while working at IBM. The paper established systematic methods for analyzing and transforming programs so compilers could produce more efficient machine instructions.

Weizenbaum published a paper explaining how ELIZA processed language to produce a conversation. The exchange could resemble human dialogue even though the program’s language handling remained superficial.
Nixdorf’s company developed the Logatronic into the System 820 under Otto Müller’s technical leadership. A direct sales network offered the small business computer to midsize companies.
Engelbart presented NLS at the Fall Joint Computer Conference. The live production combined mouse control, linked information, collaborative editing, and graphical interaction.
Dijkstra built the THE multiprogramming system as a layered operating system. Its levels separated functions, while software-based paged virtual memory managed the computer’s storage.
Dijkstra published Go To Statement Considered Harmful in Communications of the ACM. He argued that unrestricted jumps made programs harder to understand and verify.

historical_context.title: Sputnik Launch
historical_context.description: The Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, the first artificial satellite, into Earth orbit in 1957. The U.S. response created and expanded advanced research funding that supported Douglas Engelbart's work on interactive computing at SRI.

chapters.lead_in: Stored programs turned electronic machines into systems that could change tasks through instructions. Languages, operating methods, and interactive controls expanded who could use them and what they could do.

chapters.title: Software Reaches the Public (1970-1984)

person_events.theme_connection: Allen published Control Flow Analysis and A Basis for Program Optimization at IBM. The papers used intervals to organize data-flow analysis and guide automatic compiler optimization.

Weizenbaum formulated questions later called the Weizenbaum Test. They asked whether an artificial-intelligence application would benefit society and whether it should be built, while reserving moral authority for people.
Dijkstra published A Discipline of Programming. The book treated program construction as mathematical reasoning and set out methods for proving that a program met its requirements.

person_events.event_title: Publishes Computer Power and Human Reason
person_events.theme_connection: Weizenbaum published Computer Power and Human Reason. He argued that computers could supply information while people retained responsibility for moral decisions.
Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak introduced the Apple II at the West Coast Computer Faire. Wozniak designed the machine, while Jobs helped shape its case and presented it to individual buyers.
Allen led IBM’s PTRAN parallel-computing project. Her team used program-dependence graphs to find work that compilers could distribute across parallel hardware.
Steve Jobs introduced the Macintosh at Apple’s annual shareholders meeting. Its graphical interface used pictures, windows, and menus controlled with a mouse.

chapters.lead_in: Researchers made programs easier to analyze, optimize, and verify. Personal computers carried graphical interaction into a consumer market while critics defined limits for machine authority.

chapters.title: Computing in the Pocket (2001-2007)

person_events.theme_connection: Jobs introduced the iPod at Apple headquarters in Cupertino. The portable digital music player carried Apple’s computing and industrial design into personal media.
Jobs unveiled the iPhone at Macworld in San Francisco. The touch-controlled device combined a phone, internet browser, camera, and iPod music player.

chapters.lead_in: Portable media and communication products placed networked computing into daily routines. A music player and a touch-controlled phone condensed decades of hardware and interface work into personal devices.

conclusion.text: Across these lives, the computer acquired programmable instructions, electronic memory, dependable software, conversational behavior, and direct controls for ordinary users. Each gain widened the decisions that could be expressed as machine operations. The same history produced a lasting warning. People still had to decide which judgments should remain human.

circles.title: Engine and Algorithm
circles.text: Ada Lovelace met Charles Babbage at his London soirée in 1833 after her mathematics tutor Mary Somerville introduced them. Lovelace became Babbage’s friend and collaborator on the Analytical Engine. Their correspondence informed the extensive notes she added to her translation of Luigi Menabrea’s account of the machine.

circles.title: A Published Influence
circles.text: Douglas Engelbart read Vannevar Bush’s As We May Think after its publication in 1945. Bush’s proposal for linked access to stored knowledge shaped Engelbart’s work on computer-supported human cooperation. That work led to the mouse and the NLS system.

circles.title: Across Theory and Industry
circles.text: John von Neumann credited Alan Turing’s paper with the central concept of the modern computer and sought to hire him as a postdoctoral assistant. A memoir by Heinz Billing reports that Turing and Konrad Zuse attended a meeting of British and German computing researchers. Zuse later became a frequent guest of Heinz Nixdorf in Paderborn. Their companies discussed transferring Zuse software to Nixdorf computers, but the proposed arrangement failed.

events.event_title: Lovelace Publishes Her Analytical Engine Notes

stops.title: The Programmable Idea
stops.text: Charles Babbage conceived the Difference Engine in London and later designed the Analytical Engine there. Ada Lovelace published her Analytical Engine notes in the city. More than a century after Babbage’s first design, Alan Turing drafted the stored-program Automatic Computing Engine in London.

stops.title: Counting a Nation
stops.text: Herman Hollerith received his statistical-processing patent in Washington. His punched-card machines processed the national censuses of 1890 and 1900 there. He later introduced a rewirable tabulator that could be configured for different data jobs.

stops.title: Programs During War
stops.text: Konrad Zuse built the mechanical Z1 in his parents’ Berlin apartment. He presented the relay-based Z3 in the city and developed Plankalkül while working on his next computer. Wartime conditions restricted publication and disrupted the work.

stops.title: Searching Enigma Settings
stops.text: At Bletchley Park, Alan Turing specified the bombe for searching possible Enigma settings. He also led Hut 8, which worked on German naval messages. Machinery and statistical methods reduced the number of settings cryptanalysts had to examine.

stops.title: Computing Before the Public
stops.text: Douglas Engelbart presented NLS to a conference audience in San Francisco. Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak later introduced the Apple II at the West Coast Computer Faire there. Jobs returned to San Francisco to unveil the iPhone.

opening.text: On December 9, 1968, Douglas Engelbart sat before an audience in San Francisco and operated a computer in Menlo Park through a live video link. His NLS system let him move through linked information with a mouse and edit material with distant colleagues. Bill English directed the technical production while members of Engelbart’s laboratory joined remotely.

description.text: Computing is the use of machines to represent information and follow defined instructions. At the start of the nineteenth century, calculation was human labor performed with written tables and simple tools. Mechanical engines could automate repeated operations, but building a general machine required ways to store information and control a sequence of steps. Punched cards later carried data through business and government offices. Electronic components made machines faster during the twentieth century, while stored programs allowed instructions to reside in memory. Programming languages opened those systems to a wider range of work. Interactive screens and pointing devices changed how people controlled them. By the early twenty-first century, portable products combined communication, media, and network access in devices used throughout daily life.

timeline.text: A computing idea could wait decades for materials, money, or an urgent use. National census bureaus created demand for rapid processing of millions of records. World War II accelerated work on codebreaking and military calculation while disrupting research across Europe. After the war, universities, government laboratories, and computer companies built electronic systems around stored instructions. The launch of Sputnik 1 expanded United States support for advanced research, including work on interactive computing. Business customers then created a market for smaller systems. Consumer electronics carried the resulting methods into homes and pockets. The sequence follows how each practical need exposed the next problem that machines and programs had to solve.

network.text: Computing grew through correspondence, published papers, scientific gatherings, government projects, and commercial laboratories. London soirées could connect private mathematical study with an inventor’s workshop. Technical reports crossed national borders and reached researchers who had never worked together. Wartime programs placed theorists beside engineers under strict institutional control. Postwar computer companies gathered programmers around machines that were still being designed. Conferences and professional visits later joined researchers from different national industries. Some relationships became close collaborations. Others consisted of a paper read at the right time, a single reported meeting, or a proposed business arrangement that failed. Those different forms of contact carried ideas between generations and systems.

map.text: Computing work gathered where institutions could supply records, machinery, skilled workers, and money. A capital’s scientific society supported early mechanical designs. The United States Census Office offered a national body of data and a government customer for tabulating equipment. Wartime codebreaking drew specialized workers into a secure British center, while German engineering proceeded under the pressures of war. Later, research institutes and electronics companies clustered near growing technology markets. Large conferences gave experimental systems and consumer products their first public audiences. The resulting geography contains repeated returns to a few cities, with each return placing a different kind of machine before a new group of users.

composition.throughline: Computing developed through a long transfer of ideas from mechanical calculation to programmable electronic systems and personal devices. Each stage solved a new problem of scale, control, access, or human interaction. Connections among researchers carried several ideas forward, while governments, laboratories, businesses, and conferences concentrated the work in a few places.
